query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a nanoscale interfacial coating at the internal lamellar boundaries of eutectic high-entropy alloys will simultaneously enhance room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by improving interfacial cohesion and load transfer while delaying microcrack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as crack nucleation sites under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Localized deposition or in situ reactive modification to apply a nanoscale ceramic/oxide interfacial coating.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading on specimens processed with the engineered interfacial modification.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale interfacial coatings that alter the chemistry and structure at the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The coating enhances interfacial bonding to reduce stress concentration and delay microcrack nucleation, thereby improving effective load transfer across the phases and boosting both strength and ductility relative to the uncoated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline unmodified alloy, the treated alloy should exhibit a statistically significant increase in ultimate tensile strength and uniform elongation, demonstrating improved ductility and resistance to catastrophic crack propagation.
generation.baseline: Conventional, unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows brittle failure and limited tensile ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable under room-temperature tensile deformation in eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures; outcomes may differ under alternative loading conditions or for different alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of strength and ductility improvement may depend on coating thickness, adhesion quality, and potential unintended microstructural alterations, which remain to be optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the nanoscale interfacial coating applied by localized deposition or in situ reaction, and a control set with no coating. Subject both sets to identical room-temperature tensile tests while monitoring crack initiation and propagation through microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility (i.e., uniform elongation) compared to the unmodified control, or if the coating results in adverse microstructural changes leading to early failure, then the hypothesis is falsified.
